ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.formatted: Fourth, in <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref>, participants were presented with questions and instructed to read the passage to answer them, but were not required to provide answers before reading.

table.text: Participants were recruited from the Boston College SONA participant pool and received course credit.
One participant had eyetracking data for fewer than all four pages of the text and was excluded.
Four participants had no final test data and were excluded.
At the beginning of the session, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions.
Participants had unlimited time to respond and clicked a triangle at the bottom of the screen to advance to the next question.
Before reading, participants completed Tobii Pro Lab's nine-point calibration procedure, which presented white targets against a grey background.
After reading, all participants completed a president recognition task (https://run. pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preq_president) that served as a distractor and lasted approximately 3 minutes.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The target sample size was determined based on the specific benefit of prequestions. A recent meta-analysis reported a medium-sized effect (g = 0. 54; St. Hilaire et al. (2024)), which we converted to an odds ratio of 2.66 for the preregistered binomial mixed-effects model. A simulation-based power analysis using mixedpower (Kumle et al., 2021), informed by pilot data, indicated that 45 participants per condition would provide 90% power to detect an effect of this magnitude. We therefore planned to recruit 135 participants, with 45 assigned to each of the three conditions.

In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

table.sample_size_rationale: Based on a recent meta-analysis, the specific effect of prequestions has a medium effect size (g = .54 ; St. Hilaire et al., 2023). This translates to an OR of 2.663 and a log odds of .979. This information was used to run a  generalized linear mixed model power simulation with pilot data using the mixed package in R. Our simulation results suggest we need 45 participants for 90% power to detect a medium sized effect. Because we are using 3 groups, not 2, and are also analyzing eye tracking measures we plan to run 135 participants (45 in each group).

table.statistical_tests:
For final test performance, a fully maximal generalized linear mixed model will be used with a binomial logit link. We are modeling points earned / total points for each topic category (12).  We did not model at the specific question level as there appeared to be issues with model fit. Modeling points received/ total produced more desirable model fits. 

glmer(cbind(points earned, total-points_earned)~group*topic, (1+topic|participant), family=binomial)

A statistical model that is meant for proportional data with 0s and 1s might be best here. One such model is the ordered beta model. 

glmmTMB(prop~group*topic, (1+topic|participant) + (1|question), family=ordbeta)

For eye tracking measures, a lmer model will be run with fixation duration, first-pass duration, and re-reading duration: 

lmer(fix_durarion~group*topic, (1+topic|participant))

If fixation duration is heavily skewed we will use an ex-gaussian distribution.  If we go with this model, we will use the brms package in R and use weakly informative priors. Our focus will be on the mu or mean of the distribution

bform_exg1 <- bf(
rt ~ group*topic + (1 + topic |p| participant) 
sigma ~ group*topic  + (1 + topic |p|participant)
beta ~ group*topic + (1 +  topic|p| participant)
)

fit_exg1 <- brm(
bform_exg1, data = data
warmup = 1000,
                    iter = 5000,
                    chains = 4,
                    prior = prior_exp1,
                    family = exgaussian(),
                    inits = 0,
                    cores =4, 
control = list(adapt_delta = 0.8), 
backend="cmdstanr", 
threads = threading(4))

For first-pass regression, we will use a multilevel logistic regression 

glmer(regression(0 = no 1 = yes)~group*topic, (1+topic|participant)  + (1|sentence), family=binomial)

We will also test the specific effect of prequestions by combining the TB and Polio groups 
 and comparing them to the control group (Prequestions vs. No Prequestions).

table.research_questions:
In a prequestion study, three key comparisons are typically made. First, what is the overall score on the post-test for the Prequestion Group compared to the Control Group? This gives us an idea of the overall benefit of prequestions for enhancing learning. Second, what is the Prequestion Group’s score on the post-test specifically for prequestioned information, compared to the Control Group’s overall post-test score on the entire set of questions? This gives us a closer look at the benefits of prequestions by focusing on learning of the information from the lesson that was specifically addressed in the prequestions. If prequestions enhance learning of information that was specifically addressed in those prequestions, this can be referred to as the “specific benefit” of prequestions. Finally, what is the Prequestion Group’s score on the post-test for non-prequestioned information, compared to the Control Group’s overall post-test score on the entire set of questions? This gives us an idea of whether the benefits of prequestions generalize to information from the lesson that was not addressed in the prequestions. As such, this can be referred to as the “general benefit” of prequestions. As described below, the research on prequestions sometimes shows specific benefits, sometimes general benefits, and sometimes both. We predict that prequestioned groups will show a specific effect for the information they were pretested on (TB or Polio), but not a general benefit.

Eye tracking

- We predict that prequestioned information will result in longer gaze durations and longe re-reading durations  back to the prequestioned information compared to non-prequestioned information. Specifically, those in the TB group should show longer gaze durations on TB prequestions than Polio questions. The opposite should be observed for the Polio group. We do not expect there to be a difference in eye tracking measures for the control.

First, what is the overall score on the post-test for the Prequestion Group compared to the Control Group? This gives us an idea of the overall benefit of prequestions for enhancing learning. Second, what is the Prequestion Group’s score on the post-test specifically for prequestioned information, compared to the Control Group’s overall post-test score on the entire set of questions? This gives us a closer look at the benefits of prequestions by focusing on learning of the information from the lesson that was specifically addressed in the prequestions. If prequestions enhance learning of information that was specifically addressed in those prequestions, this can be referred to as the “specific benefit” of prequestions. Finally, what is the Prequestion Group’s score on the post-test for non-prequestioned information, compared to the Control Group’s overall post-test score on the entire set of questions? This gives us an idea of whether the benefits of prequestions generalize to information from the lesson that was not addressed in the prequestions. As such, this can be referred to as the “general benefit” of prequestions. As described below, the research on prequestions sometimes shows specific benefits, sometimes general benefits, and sometimes both. We predict that prequestioned groups will show a specific effect for the information they were pretested on (TB or Polio), but not a general benefit.

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 11757 columns across 350 data files.
#### Issues Identified

739 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.
#### Spreadsheet Formatting
We examined 5 spreadsheet files in the repository; 3 have at least one formatting issue.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 350 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Fourth, in Lewis and Mensink (2012), participants were presented with questions and instructed to read the passage to answer them, but were not required to provide answers before reading.
Participants were recruited from the Boston College SONA participant pool and received course credit.
One participant had eyetracking data for fewer than all four pages of the text and was excluded.
Four participants had no final test data and were excluded.
At the beginning of the session, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions.
Participants had unlimited time to respond and clicked a triangle at the bottom of the screen to advance to the next question.
Before reading, participants completed Tobii Pro Lab's nine-point calibration procedure, which presented white targets against a grey background.
After reading, all participants completed a president recognition task (https://run. pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preq_president) that served as a distractor and lasted approximately 3 minutes.
Participants completed a final test consisting of all ten short-answer questions (five about polio and five about TB), presented in random order (https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preQ_ test).
Participants were then thanked and debriefed.

report:
This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 25 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:25, File = c("split_qs2.R", "_targets.R", 
"bayes_helpers.R", "bf_sensitivity.R", "derive_et_measures.R", 
"download_models.R", "export_brms_cache.R", "eye_tracking.qmd", 
"eye_tracking.R", "grade_prequestions.R", "grade_test.R", "data.R", 
"final_test.qmd", "final_test.R", "make_ra_scoring_sheet.R", 
"manuscript_inputs.R", "Power_Analysis_Pilot_Data.Rmd", "power_analysis.qmd", 
"prequestions.qmd", "prequestions.R", "rater_agreement.R", "manuscript.qmd", 
"scoring_rubric.R", "setup.R", "manuscript_helpers.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", 
"—", "grade_prequestions.R, grade_test.R", "grade_test.R", 
"grade_test.R", "grade_prequestions.R, grade_test.R", "grade_prequestions.R", 
"—", "—", "grade_prequestions.R", "grade_prequestions.R", 
"—", "manuscript_inputs.R, rater_agreement.R", "—", "—", 
"setup.R"), Basis = c("numeric", "none", "none", "none", "none", 
"none", "none", "none", "none", "none", "none", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "none", 
"none", "dependency", "dependency", "none", "dependency", "none", 
"none", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -25L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
**3 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `split_qs2.R` to `scripts/split_qs2.R` (in export_brms_cache.R); `scoring_rubric.R` to `scripts/scoring_rubric.R` (in grade_prequestions.R); `scoring_rubric.R` to `scripts/scoring_rubric.R` (in grade_test.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 2 references matched several files sharing a name and could not be resolved by study group or folder; they were left unrewritten and flagged. **6 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 25 scripts: 10 ran without error, 11 errored, 0 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script needs the internet**, which is off during the run: download_models.R. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `manuscript_helpers.R` after `setup.R`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. **1 script stopped on a file another script writes**, so it was run once more after the other scripts: `grade_test.R` (scoring_rubric.R). Then this one ran to the end: `grade_test.R`. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **2 scripts looked for 2 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `scripts/split_qs2.R` to `scripts/scripts/split_qs2.R` for `export_brms_cache.R`; `scripts/scoring_rubric.R` to `scripts/scripts/scoring_rubric.R` for `grade_prequestions.R`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first; a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("split_qs2.R", "_targets.R", "bayes_helpers.R", 
"bf_sensitivity.R", "derive_et_measures.R", "download_models.R", 
"export_brms_cache.R", "eye_tracking.qmd", "eye_tracking.R", 
"grade_prequestions.R", "grade_test.R", "data.R", "final_test.qmd", 
"final_test.R", "make_ra_scoring_sheet.R", "manuscript_helpers.R", 
"manuscript_inputs.R", "Power_Analysis_Pilot_Data.Rmd", "power_analysis.qmd", 
"prequestions.qmd", "prequestions.R", "rater_agreement.R", "manuscript.qmd", 
"scoring_rubric.R", "setup.R"), Outcome = c("ran_ok", "ran_ok", 
"errored", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", "needs_internet", "errored", "errored", 
"errored", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", "dependency_unavailable", "errored", 
"errored", "errored", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", "dependency_unavailable", 
"dependency_unavailable", "errored", "errored", "errored", "errored", 
"ran_ok", "ran_ok"), Detail = c("", "", "undefined_variable", 
"", "", "", "runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "", "", "dependency_unavailable", 
"runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "", "", "dependency_unavailable", 
"dependency_unavailable", "runtime", "runtime", "undefined_variable", 
"runtime", "", ""), "Time (s)" = c(0.6, 1.4, 3.2, 4.7, 76.8, 
0.7, 0.8, 4.7, 4.7, 3.1, 3.8, 1.9, 4.6, 4.5, 1.4, 3.5, 7.5, 0.7, 
2.9, 4.6, 4.7, 1.5, 3.8, 1.7, 3.7)), row.names = c(NA, -25L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**
**2 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false
```

I thank Shana Carpenter for help with the materials and with conceptualizing the study.
A common study strategy involves retrieving information from memory by answering questions after a learning event (Hartwig & Dunlosky, 2012).
text.formatted: A common study strategy involves retrieving information from memory by answering questions after a learning event <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hartwig & Dunlosky, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This technique, known as retrieval practice, has been shown to improve long-term retention across a wide range of materials and learning contexts, a phenomenon known as the testing effect (S. K. Carpenter, 2012; Dunlosky et al., 2013; Kornell & Vaughn, 2016; Roediger & Karpicke, 2006; Rowland, 2014).
text.formatted: This technique, known as retrieval practice, has been shown to improve long-term retention across a wide range of materials and learning contexts, a phenomenon known as the testing effect (S. K. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Carpenter, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Dunlosky et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kornell & Vaughn, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Roediger & Karpicke, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Rowland, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Surprisingly, answering questions before a learning event can also improve subsequent memory, even when learners have little prior knowledge of the material and most of their initial answers are incorrect.
This phenomenon, known as the prequestion effect, is particularly intriguing because, unlike traditional retrieval practice, it does not require learners to retrieve previously studied information.

Although this finding is consistent with the broader literature suggesting that effortful and even error-prone learning experiences can benefit long-term retention (Bjork, 1994), why prequestions improve learning remains unclear.
text.formatted: Although this finding is consistent with the broader literature suggesting that effortful and even error-prone learning experiences can benefit long-term retention <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bjork, 1994)</ref>, why prequestions improve learning remains unclear.

text.text: The benefits of prequestions are typically demonstrated in experiments in which learners are assigned to a prequestion group or a control group (S. K. Carpenter et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The benefits of prequestions are typically demonstrated in experiments in which learners are assigned to a prequestion group or a control group (S. K. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Carpenter et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Before encountering the learning material, the prequestion group attempts to answer questions about the upcoming content, often guessing when they do not know the answers, whereas the control group encounters the material without answering any questions.
After learning, both groups complete a final memory test assessing information that was targeted by the prequestions as well as information that was not.

The typical finding is that learners who received prequestions remember the targeted information better than those who did not, a phenomenon known as the specific benefit of prequestions (Pan & Carpenter, 2023).
text.formatted: The typical finding is that learners who received prequestions remember the targeted information better than those who did not, a phenomenon known as the specific benefit of prequestions <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Pan & Carpenter, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In some cases, prequestions also improve memory for information that was not directly targeted, known as a general benefit of prequestions.
However, whereas the specific benefit is robust, the general benefit is less consistent.

Two recent meta-analyses found substantial specific benefits (g = 0.54, St. Hilaire et al., 2024; g = 0.66, King-Shepard et al., 2025), but no reliable general benefit (g = 0.04, St. Hilaire et al., 2024; g = 0.01, King-Shepard et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Two recent meta-analyses found substantial specific benefits (g = 0.54, <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">St. Hilaire et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">g = 0.66, King-Shepard et al., 2025)</ref>, but no reliable general benefit (g = 0.04, <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">St. Hilaire et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">g = 0.01, King-Shepard et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, some studies have reported general benefits depending on the learning materials (S. K. Carpenter & Toftness, 2017), the types of questions used (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; St. Hilaire et al., 2019), and the placement of non-prequestioned information relative to prequestioned content (Sana & Carpenter, 2023).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, some studies have reported general benefits depending on the learning materials (S. K. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Carpenter & Toftness, 2017)</ref>, the types of questions used <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">St. Hilaire et al., 2019)</ref>, and the placement of non-prequestioned information relative to prequestioned content <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Sana & Carpenter, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The specific benefit, by contrast, has been demonstrated acorss a wide variety of study materials and settings (S. K. Carpenter et al., 2018; S. K. Carpenter & Toftness, 2017; Geller et al., 2017; Richland et al., 2009; Soderstrom & Bjork, 2023; St. Hilaire & Carpenter, 2020; see Pan & Carpenter, 2023 for a review).
text.formatted: The specific benefit, by contrast, has been demonstrated acorss a wide variety of study materials and settings (S. K. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Carpenter et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">S. K. Carpenter & Toftness, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Geller et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Richland et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Soderstrom & Bjork, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">St. Hilaire & Carpenter, 2020</ref>; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Pan & Carpenter, 2023</ref> for a review).

text.text: Why do preqeustions improve learning?
Several non-mutually exclusive mechanisms have been proposed (King-Shepard et al., 2025; Pan & Carpenter, 2023).
text.formatted: Several non-mutually exclusive mechanisms have been proposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(King-Shepard et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Pan & Carpenter, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Prequestions may stimulate curiosity about the answers (Berlyne, 1954 (Berlyne, , 1962)), encourage elaboration by activating related prior knowledge (Kornell et al., 2009), or provide a metacognitive "reality check" that makes learners aware of gaps in their knowledge (Bjork et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Prequestions may stimulate curiosity about the answers <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Berlyne, 1954</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Berlyne, , 1962))</ref>, encourage elaboration by activating related prior knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kornell et al., 2009)</ref>, or provide a metacognitive "reality check" that makes learners aware of gaps in their knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bjork et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Although these explanations differ, they share the possibility that prequestions direct learners' attention toward information relevant to the questions (King-Shepard et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Although these explanations differ, they share the possibility that prequestions direct learners' attention toward information relevant to the questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(King-Shepard et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: According to an attentionbased account, prequestions signal which information is important, encouraging learners to attend to and process that information more thoroughly when they encounter it (Pan & Carpenter, 2023).
text.formatted: According to an attentionbased account, prequestions signal which information is important, encouraging learners to attend to and process that information more thoroughly when they encounter it <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Pan & Carpenter, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this account, researchers looking at eye movements during a learning episode have found that learners spend more time looking at (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; Yang et al., 2021), re-inspecting, and returning to prequestioned information after reading subsequent material (Lewis & Mensink, 2012).
text.formatted: Consistent with this account, researchers looking at eye movements during a learning episode have found that learners spend more time looking at <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Yang et al., 2021)</ref>, re-inspecting, and returning to prequestioned information after reading subsequent material <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Lewis & Mensink, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Although these findings support an attention-based account, several results suggest that directing attention toward prequestioned information may not, by itself, fully explain the benefits of prequestions.
If prequestions primarily function by signaling which information deserves attention, other methods of highlighting that information might be expected to produce similar benefits.

However, answering prequestions has been found to improve memory more than studying material with the tested concepts emphasized or reading questions without answering them (Richland et al., 2009), and more than reading learning objectives or statements of the target facts (Sana et al., 2020; but see Rivers et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, answering prequestions has been found to improve memory more than studying material with the tested concepts emphasized or reading questions without answering them <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Richland et al., 2009)</ref>, and more than reading learning objectives or statements of the target facts <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Sana et al., 2020</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Rivers et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, although prequestions reliably improve memory for targeted information (King-Shepard et al., 2025; St. Hilaire et al., 2024), some studies also find benefits for information that was not prequestioned (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; Rivers et al., 2026; Sana & Carpenter, 2023; St. Hilaire et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Moreover, although prequestions reliably improve memory for targeted information <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(King-Shepard et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">St. Hilaire et al., 2024)</ref>, some studies also find benefits for information that was not prequestioned <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Rivers et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Sana & Carpenter, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">St. Hilaire et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Any account of the prequestion effect must therefore consider why learning benefits are sometimes restricted to prequestioned information and sometimes extend to other material.
One account that may be able to explain these differences is the attentional-window account (Sana & Carpenter, 2023).
text.formatted: One account that may be able to explain these differences is the attentional-window account <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Sana & Carpenter, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: According to this account, prequestions initiate a period of heightened attention as learners search for the answers, with attention returning to baseline once the relevant information has been encountered.
Information presented while this attentional window remains open may also benefit, even if it was not directly targeted by a prequestion.
Thus, whether prequestions produce a general benefit should depend partly on where the prequestioned information appears in the learning material.
Supporting this prediction, Sana and Carpenter (2023) found that prequestions produced only a specific benefit when the targeted information appeared near the beginning of a passage.
text.formatted: Supporting this prediction, <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Sana and Carpenter (2023)</ref> found that prequestions produced only a specific benefit when the targeted information appeared near the beginning of a passage.

text.text: However, when the targeted information appeared near the end, prequestions also improved memory for non-prequestioned information encountered while learners were presumably still searching for the answers.
These findings suggest that the effects of prequestions may depend on how attention is allocated throughout the learning event.
Nevertheless, much of the evidence for this account comes from subsequent memory performance rather than direct observations of processing during learning.
Eye tracking provides a way to examine these attentional predictions as learning unfolds.
During reading and visual exploration, the eyes alternate between relatively brief periods of stability, known as fixations, and rapid movements between them, known as saccades.

The location and duration of fixations provide measures of overt visual attention and are sensitive to cognitive processes involved in comprehension and learning (Deng & Gao, 2023; Hyönä et al., 2003; Madsen et al., 2021; Rayner, 1998; Rayner, 2009).
text.formatted: The location and duration of fixations provide measures of overt visual attention and are sensitive to cognitive processes involved in comprehension and learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Deng & Gao, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hyönä et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Madsen et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Rayner, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rayner, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Because eye movements can be recorded continuously without interrupting the learning experience, eye tracking allows researchers to examine how learners visually process information as they encounter it rather than inferring processing solely from subsequent memory performance (Rayner, 1998).
text.formatted: Because eye movements can be recorded continuously without interrupting the learning experience, eye tracking allows researchers to examine how learners visually process information as they encounter it rather than inferring processing solely from subsequent memory performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Rayner, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, eye movements can distinguish processing during an initial encounter with information from subsequent reprocessing, such as rereading a sentence or returning to an earlier part of a passage.

Eye-movement measures are also sensitive to individual differences in reading ability (Ashby et al., 2005; Perfetti, 2007), prior knowledge (McNamara & Magliano, 2009), and working memory capacity (Daneman & Carpenter, 1980).
text.formatted: Eye-movement measures are also sensitive to individual differences in reading ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ashby et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Perfetti, 2007)</ref>, prior knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(McNamara & Magliano, 2009)</ref>, and working memory capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Daneman & Carpenter, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, real-time measures such as eye tracking have been identified as an important direction for prequestion research (Pan & Carpenter, 2023).
text.formatted: Accordingly, real-time measures such as eye tracking have been identified as an important direction for prequestion research <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Pan & Carpenter, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, King-Shepard et al. (2025) recommended examining how prequestions influence the time learners spend processing prequestioned and non-prequestioned information during reading.
text.formatted: In particular, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">King-Shepard et al. (2025)</ref> recommended examining how prequestions influence the time learners spend processing prequestioned and non-prequestioned information during reading.

text.text: Relatively few studies have used eye tracking to investigate how prequestions influence reading.

In an early study, readers who received questions before reading spent more time rereading and carefully processing question-related information while reading unrelated material more quickly (Rothkopf & Billington, 1979). Lewis and Mensink (2012) examined the effects of prequestions in two eye-tracking experiments using passages on different topics.
text.formatted: In an early study, readers who received questions before reading spent more time rereading and carefully processing question-related information while reading unrelated material more quickly <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Rothkopf & Billington, 1979)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref> examined the effects of prequestions in two eye-tracking experiments using passages on different topics.

text.text: In Experiment 1, participants read a passage about space travel after receiving one of two sets of six prequestions or no prequestions.

Readers receiving one set of prequestions spent more time re-inspecting and looking back to question-relevant sentences and subsequently recalled more of that information than readers receiving the other set.
However, the second set of prequestions did not produce reliable effects on reading or memory.
In Experiment 2, Lewis and Mensink (2012) used a passage describing the humanitarian efforts of the Gates Foundation, including efforts to address polio and tuberculosis (TB).
text.formatted: In Experiment 2, <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref> used a passage describing the humanitarian efforts of the Gates Foundation, including efforts to address polio and tuberculosis (TB).

text.text: One group received four prequestions about TB before reading, whereas a control group read the passage without prequestions.
Eye movements were recorded using a head-mounted eye tracker.
Prequestions did not increase forward reading times for sentences containing the answers.

Instead, readers who received prequestions spent more time rereading the targeted sentences before moving forward and made more look-backs to those sentences after proceeding to later portions of the passage.
They also showed a smaller increase in look-backs to other parts of the text.

On a subsequent free-recall test, the prequestion group recalled approximately twice as much of the targeted information as the control group, but did not recall more of the non-prequestioned information.
Thus, the specific memory benefit was accompanied by greater reprocessing of the targeted sentences rather than slower initial reading.
This pattern suggests that readers may first recognize information as relevant to a prequestion and subsequently return to process it more extensively.
More recently, Bostan and Ozcelik (2026) examined the effects of integrative prequestions, which require learners to combine information from different parts of a text.
text.formatted: More recently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bostan and Ozcelik (2026)</ref> examined the effects of integrative prequestions, which require learners to combine information from different parts of a text.

text.text: Twelve participants received integrative prequestions before reading a passage about car brakes, whereas another twelve read the passage without prequestions.
Compared with the control group, readers who received prequestions made more fixations, spent more time on targeted sentences, and made more transitions between them.

Unlike most prequestion studies, the authors also observed a general benefit: participants who received prequestions performed better on questions assessing non-prequestioned information despite spending less time fixating those sentences.

These findings suggest that prequestions can alter the distribution of visual processing across a passage, although increased fixation time on particular information does not necessarily correspond to greater memory for that information.

Taken together, previous eye-tracking studies indicate that prequestions influence how learners allocate visual attention during reading (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; Lewis & Mensink, 2012; Yang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Taken together, previous eye-tracking studies indicate that prequestions influence how learners allocate visual attention during reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis & Mensink, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Yang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, whether these changes contribute directly to improved memory or reflect other processes initiated by prequestions remains uncertain.
Furthermore, some findings suggest that the benefits of prequestions cannot be explained simply by the amount of time learners spend processing the material.

For example, in a large multisite classroom study, prequestions improved learning even though students subsequently watched less of the instructional videos, with some students skipping the videos entirely (Motz et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, in a large multisite classroom study, prequestions improved learning even though students subsequently watched less of the instructional videos, with some students skipping the videos entirely <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Motz et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, Bostan and Ozcelik (2026) found improved memory for non-prequestioned information despite shorter fixation times on that information.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bostan and Ozcelik (2026)</ref> found improved memory for non-prequestioned information despite shorter fixation times on that information.

text.text: Such findings suggest that prequestions may influence not only the allocation of attention but also how information is processed once encountered.
One alternative explanation is the mental model hypothesis proposed by Motz et al. (2026).
text.formatted: One alternative explanation is the mental model hypothesis proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Motz et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: According to this account, prequestions activate relevant prior knowledge before learning, facilitating the processing and encoding of related information when it is subsequently encountered.
As learners recognize connections between the new information and their activated knowledge, they may allocate additional attention to that content.
From this perspective, increased attention may follow the recognition of relevant information rather than being the primary mechanism responsible for improved learning.

Consistent with this possibility, Motz et al. (2026) found that the benefit of prequestions was greater among students who answered more prequestions correctly, suggesting that access to relevant prior knowledge may contribute to the effect.
text.formatted: Consistent with this possibility, <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Motz et al. (2026)</ref> found that the benefit of prequestions was greater among students who answered more prequestions correctly, suggesting that access to relevant prior knowledge may contribute to the effect.

text.text: Although the attention-based and mental model accounts are not necessarily mutually exclusive, they raise an important question about the timing and nature of the processing changes associated with prequestions.

In particular, determining whether prequestions influence reading when relevant information is first encountered or primarily during subsequent reprocessing may help clarify how prequestions shape learning.
The existing literature provides evidence that prequestions influence both memory and the allocation of visual attention during learning.
However, questions remain about when these changes in visual processing emerge, whether they are specific to prequestioned information, and how prequestions alter the distribution of reading times.
The current study addressed these questions by combining a counterbalanced prequestion design with eye-tracking measures that distinguish initial reading from subsequent reprocessing.
We also used distributional analyses to examine how prequestions influence reading times beyond differences in average duration.
Our study builds on two previous eye-tracking investigations of prequestions during reading (Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026; Lewis & Mensink, 2012) while addressing several methodological limitations.
text.formatted: Our study builds on two previous eye-tracking investigations of prequestions during reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bostan & Ozcelik, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis & Mensink, 2012)</ref> while addressing several methodological limitations.

text.text: First, in Experiment 2 of Lewis and Mensink (2012) and in Bostan and Ozcelik (2026), the same set of sentences was prequestioned for all participants in the prequestion condition.
text.formatted: First, in Experiment 2 of <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref> and in <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bostan and Ozcelik (2026)</ref>, the same set of sentences was prequestioned for all participants in the prequestion condition.

text.text: Consequently, the effects of prequestions could not be fully separated from characteristics of the particular sentences being targeted.
Although Experiment 1 of Lewis and Mensink (2012) included two sets of prequestions, these targeted different numbers of sentences, and only one set reliably affected reading.
text.formatted: Although Experiment 1 of <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref> included two sets of prequestions, these targeted different numbers of sentences, and only one set reliably affected reading.

text.text: In the current study, prequestioned content was fully counterbalanced so that the same sentences were read both with and without prequestions across participants.

Second, previous studies used relatively small samples, with approximately 20 participants per group in Lewis and Mensink (2012) and 12 participants per group in Bostan and Ozcelik (2026), limiting the precision of the estimated effects.
text.formatted: Second, previous studies used relatively small samples, with approximately 20 participants per group in <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref> and 12 participants per group in <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bostan and Ozcelik (2026)</ref>, limiting the precision of the estimated effects.

text.text: In addition, Bostan and Ozcelik (2026) compared total fixation durations and counts between groups without accounting for participant-level differences in reading behavior.

The current study included a substantially larger sample (138 participants, approximately 46 per condition) and used models that accounted for variation across participants and items, including sentences and test questions where appropriate.

Third, whereas previous studies primarily analyzed average reading or fixation times, we also examined the distribution of reading times to determine whether prequestions produce broader shifts in reading duration or disproportionately influence unusually long readings.
Fourth, in Lewis and Mensink (2012), participants were presented with questions and instructed to read the passage to answer them, but were not required to provide answers before reading.
text.formatted: Fourth, in <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref>, participants were presented with questions and instructed to read the passage to answer them, but were not required to provide answers before reading.

text.text: Although learners may have generated answers covertly, which can be as effective as overtly answering prequestions (Rivers et al., 2026), whether they did so is unknown.

text.text: In the current study, participants explicitly answered each prequestion before reading, consistent with the procedure used in many prequestion studies.

Finally, unlike the integrative questions used by Bostan and Ozcelik (2026), each prequestion in the current study targeted information contained within a single sentence, as in Lewis and Mensink (2012).

text.text: Such questions have generally been associated with specific rather than general memory benefits (St. Hilaire et al., 2019).

text.text: In out study, participants read the Gates Foundation passage used in Experiment 2 of Lewis and Mensink (2012), which describes efforts to eradicate polio and TB.
text.formatted: In out study, participants read the Gates Foundation passage used in Experiment 2 of <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref>, which describes efforts to eradicate polio and TB.

text.text: Before reading, participants answered five prequestions about polio, five prequestions about TB, or no prequestions.
The passage contained ten target sentences, each providing the answer to one prequestion.
By counterbalancing which topic was prequestioned, every target sentence served as prequestioned information for one group and non-prequestioned information for another.
This design allowed us to compare processing of the same sentences across prequestion and noprequestion conditions while minimizing confounding between prequestion status and sentence content.
We examined two categories of eye-movement measures.
Global measures, including total gaze duration, rereading time, and regressions-in (look-backs), captured processing across encounters with a sentence, including subsequent returns to it.
Our local measure, selective regression-path duration, captured processing associated with the initial encounter with a sentence, before the reader progressed to later text.
Distinguishing these measures allowed us to assess whether prequestions influence processing when relevant information is first encountered, during subsequent rereading, or both.
In addition to examining these measures, we used distributional analyses to characterize how prequestions influence reading times.
Reading and fixation durations are typically rightskewed, with a lower bound of zero and a relatively long tail of unusually long observations (Balota & Yap, 2011; Staub et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Reading and fixation durations are typically rightskewed, with a lower bound of zero and a relatively long tail of unusually long observations <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Balota & Yap, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Staub et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, statistical models that assume normally distributed reading times may not adequately characterize the observed data, and transformations intended to reduce skewness can alter the scale on which effects are evaluated (Lo & Andrews, 2015).
text.formatted: Consequently, statistical models that assume normally distributed reading times may not adequately characterize the observed data, and transformations intended to reduce skewness can alter the scale on which effects are evaluated <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lo & Andrews, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore modeled total gaze duration using the ex-Gaussian distribution, which represents response times as the sum of a Gaussian component, characterized by its mean (μ), and an exponential component, characterized by its mean (τ).

An advantage of the ex-Gaussian distribution is that it allows changes in the location of the Gaussian component to be distinguished from changes in the exponential component contributing to the right tail.

Although these parameters are descriptive and do not uniquely identify underlying cognitive processes (Matzke & Wagenmakers, 2009), previous research suggests that experimental manipulations can influence them differently.
text.formatted: Although these parameters are descriptive and do not uniquely identify underlying cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Matzke & Wagenmakers, 2009)</ref>, previous research suggests that experimental manipulations can influence them differently.

text.text: For example, word frequency has been found to affect both μ and τ in fixation durations during reading (Staub et al., 2010), whereas modest visual degradation of text primarily affected μ (White & Staub, 2012).
text.formatted: For example, word frequency has been found to affect both μ and τ in fixation durations during reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Staub et al., 2010)</ref>, whereas modest visual degradation of text primarily affected μ <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(White & Staub, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, in scene viewing, image type influenced μ, whereas familiarity increased τ, reflecting a greater contribution from longer fixations (Guy et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Similarly, in scene viewing, image type influenced μ, whereas familiarity increased τ, reflecting a greater contribution from longer fixations <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Guy et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These findings illustrate how experimental manipulations may alter different characteristics of the reading-time distribution.
This distinction may be particularly informative for understanding prequestion effects.

If prequestions lead readers to recognize particular sentences as relevant and sometimes engage in additional processing or reanalysis, they may disproportionately increase longer reading times rather than uniformly slowing reading.
Analyses of average reading duration alone cannot distinguish these possibilities.
We therefore examined both ex-Gaussian parameters.

An effect on μ would indicate a shift in the Gaussian component of the reading-time distribution, whereas an effect on τ would indicate a greater contribution from the exponential component and its right tail.
Although neither pattern provides a unique signature of a cognitive mechanism, these analyses allow a more detailed characterization of how prequestions change reading behavior.

For final test performance, we predicted a specific benefit of prequestions: participants would remember more information about the prequestioned topic than participants in the noprequestion condition.

Based on prior findings that general benefits are less consistent, particularly for questions targeting individual pieces of information (King-Shepard et al., 2025; St. Hilaire et al., 2019), we did not predict a general benefit for the non-prequestioned topic.
text.formatted: Based on prior findings that general benefits are less consistent, particularly for questions targeting individual pieces of information <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(King-Shepard et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">St. Hilaire et al., 2019)</ref>, we did not predict a general benefit for the non-prequestioned topic.

text.text: We compared performance for prequestioned and non-prequestioned information against performance for the same material in the no-prequestion condition, both overall and separately for each topic.
For eye movements, we predicted that prequestioned sentences would receive longer total gaze durations and more rereading than the same sentences encountered without prequestions.

Specifically, we expected an interaction between prequestion condition and topic, such that Polio prequestions would selectively increase processing of polio-related sentences, whereas TB prequestions would selectively increase processing of TB-related sentences.
We also examined whether these changes emerged during initial reading or subsequent reprocessing.
Finally, our distributional analyses assessed whether differences in total gaze duration were associated with changes in the Gaussian component (μ), the exponential component (τ), or both.
We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures included in the study.
The study was preregistered (https://osf.io/8env4).

The target sample size was determined based on the specific benefit of prequestions.
A recent meta-analysis reported a medium-sized effect (g = 0. 54; St. Hilaire et al. (2024)), which we converted to an odds ratio of 2.66 for the preregistered binomial mixed-effects model.

text.text: A simulation-based power analysis using mixedpower (Kumle et al., 2021), informed by pilot data, indicated that 45 participants per condition would provide 90% power to detect an effect of this magnitude.

text.text: We therefore planned to recruit 135 participants, with 45 assigned to each of the three conditions.
Participants were recruited from the Boston College SONA participant pool and received course credit.
Eye-tracking data were recorded from 161 participants.
One participant had eyetracking data for fewer than all four pages of the text and was excluded.
Eighteen participants did not meet the preregistered calibration criterion (accuracy and precision of 0.5° or better) or could not be calibrated and were excluded.
Four participants had no final test data and were excluded.
The final sample comprised 138 participants (no prequestions: 47; Polio prequestions: 45; TB prequestions: 46).
Calibration validation data were available for all included participants.
Mean calibration accuracy was 0.37° (SD = 0.10, range 0.13-0.50), and mean precision, defined as the standard deviation of gaze samples, was 0.22° (SD = 0.12, range 0.06-0.49).
All included participants with available calibration data met the preregistered criterion of 0.5° or better for both accuracy and precision.
Before reading, participants rated their familiarity with polio and tuberculosis on a scale from 0 (never heard of it) to 100 (expert).

Familiarity was low (polio: M = 24.1, SD = 16.8; tuberculosis: M = 29.4, SD = 18.8; ratings were available for 109 of the 138 participantsfoot_0 ) and similar across conditions, so the preregistered exclusion based on prior knowledge, for which no criterion had been specified, was not applied.

text.text: The passage contained 38 sentences presented across four pages, each consisting of 16-17 lines (Figure 1).

text.text: Ten sentences served as targets: five concerning polio (M = 19.4 words, SD = 11.4, range 4-35) and five concerning TB (M = 16.2 words, SD = 3.7, range 11-21).

The polio target sentences had a higher reading level than the TB target sentences, as assessed by the Flesch-Kincaid grade level (Kincaid et al., 1975), calculated using the quanteda package (Benoit et al., 2018) (polio: M = 14.1, SD = 6.2; TB: M = 8.8, SD = 2.0).

text.text: Each target sentence contained the answer to one of ten short-answer questions (five about polio and five about TB; Appendix A).
Questions required percentage-based, yes/no, or multipart responses.
The maximum possible score was 12 points per topic and 24 points overall.
The study included three conditions: polio prequestions, TB prequestions, and no prequestions.

Participants in the polio and TB conditions answered five questions about their assigned topic before reading, whereas participants in the no-prequestion condition read the passage without answering questions beforehand.

For each prequestion condition, the five target sentences corresponding to the assigned topic were classified as prequestioned, and the five sentences about the other topic were classified as non-prequestioned.

Thus, across conditions, every target sentence served as both prequestioned and non-prequestioned information, allowing the effects of prequestions to be separated from differences in sentence content.
Eye movements were recorded using a Tobii Pro Spectrum eye tracker sampling at 600 Hz.
The passage was displayed on a 23.8-inch EIZO FlexScan EV2451 monitor (1920 × 1080 pixels) viewed from approximately 65 cm without a chin rest.
Text was presented in 36-point Courier New, a monospaced font, against a grey background.
At this viewing distance, each character subtended approximately 0.5° of visual angle, and the line spacing subtended approximately 1.1°.
The experiment was administered using Tobii Pro Lab (version 25.19).
The prequestions, distractor task, and final test were programmed in PsychoPy, hosted on Pavlovia, and embedded as web elements within the Tobii Pro Lab timeline.
At the beginning of the session, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions.
The experiment consisted of four phases: prequestions, reading, a distractor task, and a final test.
Participants in the noprequestion condition skipped the prequestion phase.
Participants in the two prequestion conditions answered five short-answer questions about their assigned topic (polio or TB), presented in random order (https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller 112/preq).
text.formatted: Participants in the two prequestion conditions answered five short-answer questions about their assigned topic (polio or TB), presented in random order (<ref type="url" target="https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller">https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller</ref> 112/preq).

text.text: They were informed that they might not know the correct answers and were encouraged to provide their best guesses.
Each question appeared individually on the screen, with a text box below it for entering a response.
Participants had unlimited time to respond and clicked a triangle at the bottom of the screen to advance to the next question.
No feedback was provided.
Before reading, participants completed Tobii Pro Lab's nine-point calibration procedure, which presented white targets against a grey background.
Calibration accuracy and precision were then validated and recorded.
Participants subsequently read the four-page passage while their eye movements were recorded.
They advanced through the pages at their own pace, with no time limit, but could not return to previously viewed pages.
After reading, all participants completed a president recognition task (https://run. pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preq_president) that served as a distractor and lasted approximately 3 minutes.
text.formatted: After reading, all participants completed a president recognition task (<ref type="url" target="https://run">https://run</ref>. pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preq_president) that served as a distractor and lasted approximately 3 minutes.

text.text: Participants completed a final test consisting of all ten short-answer questions (five about polio and five about TB), presented in random order (https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preQ_ test).
text.formatted: Participants completed a final test consisting of all ten short-answer questions (five about polio and five about TB), presented in random order (<ref type="url" target="https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preQ_">https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preQ_</ref> test).

text.text: The response format was identical to that used during the prequestion phase, with unlimited response time and no feedback.
For participants in the prequestion conditions, five questions were repeated from the prequestion phase, whereas the remaining five were new.
Participants were then thanked and debriefed.
Prequestion and final-test responses were scored using a deterministic, rule-based scoring procedure developed with the assistance of Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model ID claudeopus-5-5).

Rather than scoring individual responses directly, Claude generated an R scoring script (scoring_rubric.R, used by grade_prequestions.R and grade_test.R) that applied the same predefined criteria to all responses.
The script awarded one point for each required element of a correct answer present in a participant's response.
Question-specific scoring criteria are provided in Appendix A.
To assess scoring reliability, a research assistant who was blind to experimental condition, test phase, and automated scores independently scored all 1,678 nonblank responses.
The automated and human scores agreed exactly on 97.6% of responses.

Agreement was excellent, ICC(2,1) = .99, 95% CI [.99, .99], based on a two-way random-effects, absoluteagreement, single-measure intraclass correlation coefficient (Koo & Li, 2016; Shrout & Fleiss, 1979), calculated using the irr package (Gamer et al., 2026).

text.text: All analyses used the automated scores.
Sentence-level measures were computed from the fixation-level data.
Fixations were identified with Tobii Pro Lab's Tobii I-VT (Fixation) filter, a velocity-threshold identification algorithm (Olsen, 2012; Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000), with the following settings.
text.formatted: Fixations were identified with Tobii Pro Lab's Tobii I-VT (Fixation) filter, a velocity-threshold identification algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Olsen, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000)</ref>, with the following settings.

text.text: Gaps in the gaze data shorter than 75 ms (e.g., brief losses of tracking) were filled by linear interpolation, the gaze positions of the two eyes were averaged, and noise was reduced with a moving median over a window of three samples.
A gaze sample was classified as part of a fixation when the angular velocity of the eye, computed over a 20-ms window, was below 30°/s.
Adjacent fixations separated by less than 75 ms and less than 0.5° of visual angle were merged, and fixations shorter than 60 ms were discarded.
Fixations cut off when a page appeared or disappeared can nonetheless be shorter than 60 ms in the export.
We excluded fixations shorter than 80 ms (4.0% of fixations) and longer than 1,000 ms (0.06%) before any further processing.

Both bounds follow common practice in reading research: 80 ms is the most common lower bound, and 800, 1,000, and 1,200 ms are the most common upper bounds (Schotter & Dillon, 2025; e.g., Serrano-Carot et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Both bounds follow common practice in reading research: 80 ms is the most common lower bound, and 800, 1,000, and 1,200 ms are the most common upper bounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Schotter & Dillon, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">e.g., Serrano-Carot et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Very short fixations are unlikely to reflect processing of the text and include fixations cut short by a page change.

Most fixations in reading last around 200 ms (Rayner, 1998; Schotter & Dillon, 2025); in the present data the median fixation lasted 178 ms, so a single fixation longer than 1,000 ms, 5.6 times the median, is unlikely to reflect ongoing reading and more likely reflects a lapse of attention or a brief loss of the eye-tracking signal that the fixation filter bridged.

text.text: The remaining processing (derive_et_measures.R) proceeded in four steps. (a) The exact layout of each page was reconstructed from the sentence texts and full-resolution screenshots of the pages (monospaced font, 79 characters per line), giving the screen position of every character of every sentence (Figure 1). (b) Each fixation was assigned to a text line after correcting for vertical drift, separately for each reader and page, with a procedure that combines two approaches used in automated drift-correction algorithms (Carr et al., 2022): assigning sequences of fixations to a line together, and modelling drift as a function of position on the page (details in Appendix D).
text.formatted: The remaining processing (derive_et_measures.R) proceeded in four steps. (a) The exact layout of each page was reconstructed from the sentence texts and full-resolution screenshots of the pages (monospaced font, 79 characters per line), giving the screen position of every character of every sentence (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>). (b) Each fixation was assigned to a text line after correcting for vertical drift, separately for each reader and page, with a procedure that combines two approaches used in automated drift-correction algorithms <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Carr et al., 2022)</ref>: assigning sequences of fixations to a line together, and modelling drift as a function of position on the page (details in Appendix D).

text.text: The correction was limited to the calibration accuracy criterion of 0.5° (0.57 cm, about 0.45 of a line spacing), so it could not move a reader's gaze by a whole line. (c) Each fixation was then assigned to the sentence occupying its line and horizontal position: its character column was computed from the fixed character width, a fixation on a space took the sentence of the nearest letter, and fixations more than three characters beyond either end of a line were treated as off the text. (d) Reading on each page was taken to start at the first fixation on the page's first sentence; fixations before that (the landing) contributed to total time but not to firstpass measures.
After processing, 96.8% of on-screen fixations were assigned to a sentence, and the assigned sentence agreed with Tobii Pro Lab's assignment for 89.8% of fixations.
First-pass reading was identified for 96.9% of fixated target sentences.

All measures were computed for each participant and target sentence.
Durations were divided by the number of words in the sentence (ms per word), because target sentences differed in length.
Only sentences that were fixated were analysed: a target sentence that received no fixation has no reading time, so its measures were treated as missing (17 of 1380 target sentences, 1.2%).

Following the eye-movement literature, we distinguish global measures, which reflect all processing of a sentence including later returns to it, from local measures, which reflect processing when the sentence is first encountered (Figure 3).

text.text: Eye-Movement Measures, Illustrated With a Schematic Reading Example Note.
Definitions follow Schotter and Dillon (2025).

The circles are fixations, numbered in time order (arrows: saccades; dashed arrows: regressions; dotted arrows: moves to the next line); the shaded sentence is the target, and each fixation is coloured by the measure it counts towards for the target.

Selective regression-path duration (first-pass reading; also called right-bounded reading time or selective go-past time) sums the fixations on the sentence from first entering it until the eyes first move past it to later text; fixations on earlier text during this period (here, 6) are not counted and do not end it.
Total gaze duration sums all fixations on the sentence.
Regression-in records whether the eyes returned to the sentence from later text (0/1).
Re-reading time sums the fixations on the sentence after the reader had first moved on to later text (operationalizing the preregistered "re-reading durations back to the prequestioned information").
Selective regression-path duration is defined only for sentences fixated before any later sentence (not skipped).
The duration measures do not overlap: total gaze duration is the sum of selective regression-path duration, re-reading time, and any fixations made before reading started on the page.
Global measures include later returns to the sentence; the local measure reflects processing when the sentence is first encountered.

The preregistered first-pass duration (fixations until the sentence is first exited) would here be 3 + 4 + 5 only, cut short by the brief return at 6; it was replaced by selective regression-path duration (see Statistical Analysis).
All durations were divided by the number of words in the sentence (ms per word).

Carpenter et al., 2017), run through cmdstanr (Gabry et al., 2025) with CmdStan 2.37.0.

text.text: Each target sentence, and each finaltest question, was coded by its status for the reader: prequestioned (Polio sentences and questions for readers in the Polio condition, TB sentences and questions for readers in the TB condition), non-prequestioned (the other topic for those readers), or no-prequestion (both topics for readers in the no-prequestion condition).
The main models pooled the two prequestion conditions, with Status and Topic (Polio, TB) as fixed effects.

The specific effect of prequestions was the difference prequestioned -no-prequestion: the same sentences or questions for readers whose prequestions they answered and for readers who saw no prequestions.
The general effect was non-prequestioned -no-prequestion.
Because each topic contributes equally to the prequestioned, non-prequestioned, and no-prequestion cells, differences between the Polio and TB materials cancel in these comparisons.
Both the specific and general effects and their breakdown by topic were preregistered.
To break the effects down by topic, we fitted the preregistered Group (Polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions) × Topic (Polio, TB) models with the same families and priors.

Following the preregistered hypotheses, we estimated the Polio -TB difference within each group-predicted to be positive in the Polio group, negative in the TB group, and absent in the no-prequestion group-and the Group × Topic interaction contrast, the Polio group's Polio -TB difference minus the TB group's, predicted to be positive.

Because the Polio and TB sentences (and questions) are different items, each withingroup Polio -TB difference combines any effect of prequestions with differences between the items, and with five items per topic, the population-level topic difference is estimated imprecisely.
Each within-group difference was therefore interpreted together with the interaction contrast, in which the item differences cancel because both groups read the same items.
Reading times are strongly right-skewed, so no duration was analysed with a Gaussian model.

As preregistered for heavily skewed durations, total gaze duration was analysed with an ex-Gaussian distributional model ({cogmod}; Makowski (2026)), which describes a duration as the sum of a Gaussian component, whose mean μ reflects typical reading time, and an exponential component, whose mean τ reflects the tail of unusually long readings.

The mean of an ex-Gaussian distribution is μ + τ and its standard deviation is √(σ² + τ²), where σ is the standard deviation of the Gaussian component, so μ and τ are components of reading time rather than reading times themselves.
The fixed and random effects applied to both μ and τ, and σ had by-participant random intercepts.

The preregistered first-pass duration, from first entering a sentence until first leaving it, could not be described by any of the distributions we considered (ex-Gaussian, Gamma, lognormal), because it mixes two kinds of first pass.

About half of first passes, in all three conditions, were cut short after a few fixations by a brief return to the preceding line, so the distribution had two modes: interrupted first passes of a few hundred milliseconds and complete first readings of several seconds.

First-pass reading was therefore measured as selective regression-path duration [also called right-bounded reading time; Schotter and Dillon (2025)]: the time spent on the sentence from first entering it until the eyes first moved past it to later text, so that brief returns to earlier text did not end it and time spent on earlier text was not counted (Figure 3).
text.formatted: First-pass reading was therefore measured as selective regression-path duration [also called right-bounded reading time; Schotter and Dillon (2025)]: the time spent on the sentence from first entering it until the eyes first moved past it to later text, so that brief returns to earlier text did not end it and time spent on earlier text was not counted (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Its distribution was unimodal and right-skewed and closely described by the ex-Gaussian, so it was analysed with the same ex-Gaussian model as total gaze duration (μ and τ).
Re-reading time was the time spent on a sentence after the reader had first moved on to later text, so that the two measures do not overlap (cf. rereading time in Schotter & Dillon, 2025).
text.formatted: Re-reading time was the time spent on a sentence after the reader had first moved on to later text, so that the two measures do not overlap (cf. rereading time in <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Schotter & Dillon, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Whether readers returned to a sentence from later text is captured by regressions-in (0/1), which were analysed with logistic models; re-reading time was analysed for the 37.5% of sentences that were re-read, with a Gamma model with a log link, which models positive, rightskewed durations without transforming them (Lo & Andrews, 2015); the ex-Gaussian was not suitable, because re-reading times were close to exponentially distributed, so that its Gaussian component collapsed (σ near zero).
