text.text: The model therefore describes how long readers re-read a sentence once they had returned to it.

Because the questions were worth different numbers of points (1-4), final test performance was analysed as the points earned on each question out of its maximum, with a beta-binomial model: a binomial model of the points earned with an additional parameter for overdispersion, because a participant tends to know all or none of a question's elements.
Effects are reported on the scale of the expected proportion of a question's points, which puts all questions on the same 0-1 scale.
Because each question has at most four points, scores can take only a few values (0, .25, .33, .50, .67, .75, and 1).

In posterior predictive checks, the beta-binomial model reproduced how often each score occurred (predicted and observed shares within 1.1 percentage points), better than a binomial model without overdispersion.
Prequestion performance was analysed in the same way, comparing the two prequestion conditions.
All models included the maximal random-effects structure warranted by the design (Barr et al., 2013).
text.formatted: All models included the maximal random-effects structure warranted by the design <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Topic varied within participants, so the models included by-participant random intercepts and Topic slopes (the preregistered structure).

Every target sentence and every finaltest question was prequestioned for one group, non-prequestioned for another, and read or answered by the no-prequestion group, so Status (and Group) varied within items, and the models also included by-sentence (eye movements) or by-question (final test) random intercepts and Status (or Group) slopes.
Within a participant, Status is determined by Topic, so no byparticipant Status slope was possible.
In the prequestion model, condition varied between participants and between questions, so it included random intercepts for participants and questions only.
Status, Condition, and Topic were coded with equal-prior contrasts [contr.equalprior_pairs; {bayestestR}, Makowski, Ben-Shachar, and Lüdecke (2019)].
text.formatted: Status, Condition, and Topic were coded with equal-prior contrasts <ref type="bibr">[contr.equalprior_pairs;</ref> <ref type="bibr">{bayestestR}, Makowski, Ben-Shachar, and Lüdecke (2019)</ref>].

text.text: With this coding, a normal(0, s) prior on the coefficients implies the same normal(0, s) prior on every pairwise difference between conditions, so that no condition serves as a reference with a different prior, and every comparison is tested against the same prior. s was set on each model's link scale: 1.5 on the log-odds scale (regressions-in, final test, and prequestions; an odds ratio of 4.5 for one SD), 0.5 on the log scale of the Gamma models and on the scale of τ (a factor of about 1.65 for one SD), and 100 ms per word for μ.
Intercepts, random-effect standard deviations, and correlations had weakly informative priors (Appendix B).
Each model was sampled with four chains of 10000 post-warm-up iterations (40000 posterior draws, enough for stable Bayes factors).
All models converged: there were no divergent transitions, all R-hat values were below 1.001, and all bulk effective sample sizes exceeded 4900.

Means and comparisons were computed on the response scale by averaging each posterior draw's predictions over the observed sample (modelbased with the {marginaleffects} (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024) backend and estimate = "average"), so that they incorporate the variation due to the random effects.
text.formatted: Means and comparisons were computed on the response scale by averaging each posterior draw's predictions over the observed sample (modelbased with the {marginaleffects} <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Arel-Bundock et al., 2024)</ref> backend and estimate = "average"), so that they incorporate the variation due to the random effects.

text.text: Durations are reported in ms per word, and probabilities and proportions in percent.
Effects were summarized by their posterior mean, 95% credible interval (CrI), and probability of direction (pd), the proportion of the posterior with the same sign as its median.

The pd is closely related to the frequentist p value: for a one-tailed test, p ≈ 1 -pd, and for a two-tailed test, p ≈ 2(1 -pd), so pd > 95% corresponds to a one-tailed p < .05 (Makowski, Ben-Shachar, Chen, et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The pd is closely related to the frequentist p value: for a one-tailed test, p ≈ 1 -pd, and for a two-tailed test, p ≈ 2(1 -pd), so pd > 95% corresponds to a one-tailed p < .05 <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Makowski, Ben-Shachar, Chen, et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The predictions for the specific effects and for prequestioned versus non-prequestioned material were directional (longer reading, more regressions, better recall), so we treated such an effect as present when pd > 95% in the predicted direction.
text.formatted: The predictions for the specific effects and for prequestioned versus non-prequestioned material were directional (longer reading, more regressions, better recall), so we treated such an effect as present when pd > 95% in the predicted direction.

text.text: The general effects had no directional prediction, so for them we required pd > 97.5%, corresponding to a two-tailed p < .05.

text.text: Bayes factors were not used as a decision criterion; we report them to describe the strength of the evidence for or against each effect.
Because pd only indicates the direction of an effect and cannot provide evidence that an effect is absent, we also computed Bayes factors.

Each Bayes factor compares a model in which the comparison equals 0 with one in which it is free, using the Savage-Dickey density ratio (Wagenmakers et al., 2010): the posterior density of the comparison at 0 divided by its prior density at 0.
text.formatted: Each Bayes factor compares a model in which the comparison equals 0 with one in which it is free, using the Savage-Dickey density ratio <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Wagenmakers et al., 2010)</ref>: the posterior density of the comparison at 0 divided by its prior density at 0.

text.text: The prior densities came from the same models sampled from their priors only, and both densities were computed for the comparisons on the link scale, where the equal priors apply.

For τ and for the expected re-reading time, which have no single link scale, they were computed on the response scale; for the expected re-reading time, at the population level (without random effects), because averaging over random effects drawn from their priors produced prior draws too extreme for a density estimate.

For the Group × Topic comparisons of look-backs and final test scores, the Bayes factors were also computed on the response scale (probabilities and proportions of points), the scale of the estimates.

These comparisons involve different Polio and TB items, some of which had outcomes near 0 or 1, and for such outcomes the same comparison is much less precise in log-odds than in probability, so link-scale Bayes factors could contradict the estimates.

BF10 > 3 indicates moderate, BF10 > 10 strong, BF10 > 30 very strong, and BF10 > 100 extreme evidence for a difference, and BF01 = 1/BF10 the corresponding evidence for no difference; values between 1/3 and 3 are anecdotal (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014).
text.formatted: BF10 > 3 indicates moderate, BF10 > 10 strong, BF10 > 30 very strong, and BF10 > 100 extreme evidence for a difference, and BF01 = 1/BF10 the corresponding evidence for no difference; values between 1/3 and 3 are anecdotal <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Because a Bayes factor depends on the prior, all comparisons between conditions received the same prior, and we report how sensitive the posteriors were to the priors [power-scaling sensitivity; Kallioinen et al. (2023)].

Without prequestions, readers spent on average 249 ms per word on a target sentence in total (SD = 136; about 241 words per minute), 215 ms per word (SD = 109) of it in first-pass reading (selective regression-path duration).
The ex-Gaussian estimates below divide such reading times into a typical part (μ) and a tail (τ), which sum to the mean.
We first compare prequestioned and non-prequestioned sentences with the same sentences read by no-prequestion readers (Table 1), and then test the preregistered Group × Topic crossover (Figure 5).

text.text: Prequestions changed how readers read the sentences that answered them, compared with no-prequestion readers reading the same sentences (Table 1).

text.text: During first-pass reading, measured as selective regression-path duration, typical reading time did not differ, μ: -5.0 ms per word, 95% CrI [-19.6, 9.4], pd = 75.0%, BF01 = 12.13, with strong evidence for no difference.

The tail of unusually long first-pass readings, however, was longer for prequestioned sentences, τ: 17.1 ms per word, 95% CrI [-1.4, 36.0], pd = 96.4%, BF10 = 1.25, although the Bayes factor provided only anecdotal evidence for a difference.

Total gaze duration showed the same pattern more clearly: prequestioned sentences had a longer tail, τ: 33.9 ms per word, 95% CrI [11.9, 56.4], pd = 99.9%, BF10 = 31.07, very strong evidence for a difference, whereas typical reading time did not differ, μ: 2.8 ms per word, 95% CrI [-11.4, 17.0], pd = 64.7%, BF01 = 14.26, with strong evidence for no difference.
After moving on, readers were more likely to return to prequestioned sentences from later text (37.6% vs.
30.2%), 7.3 percentage points, 95% CrI [2.4, 12.2], pd = 99.8%, BF10 = 1.67, anecdotal evidence, and when they returned, they re-read prequestioned sentences for longer (129.2 ms per word vs.
100.0 ms per word), 29.2 ms per word, 95% CrI [7.8, 51.2], pd = 99.6%, BF10 = 9.49, moderate evidence.
Non-prequestioned sentences, by contrast, were read like the same sentences in the noprequestion condition.

No measure showed a general effect (non-prequestioned -noprequestion, Table 1; all pd < 97.5%), and on every measure the Bayes factor favoured its absence (BF01 from 3.7 to 15.4), with moderate or stronger evidence on every measure.

These comparisons across groups are descriptive.
This study used eye tracking to examine how prequestions influence the allocation of visual attention during reading and whether these changes are associated with subsequent memory benefits.
On the final test, prequestions produced the expected specific benefit, with no reliable general benefit.
Participants performed better on information related to their prequestioned topic, as reflected in the Group × Topic interaction (extreme evidence).
Eye movements showed a similarly selective pattern.
Compared with the same sentences read without prequestions, prequestioned sentences exhibited a greater contribution from unusually long reading times, including during first-pass reading.
Readers also looked back to these sentences more frequently and spent more time rereading them after moving on to later material.
In contrast, processing of non-prequestioned sentences did not reliably differ from the noprequestion condition across the eye-movement measures.

The Group × Topic interaction contrast for eye movements was positive (pd > 95%) for the tail of first-pass reading (τ), the tail of total reading time (τ), look-backs from later text, and re-reading time; and not reliably positive for typical first-pass reading time (μ) and typical total reading time (μ) (Figure 5).
text.formatted: The Group × Topic interaction contrast for eye movements was positive (pd > 95%) for the tail of first-pass reading (τ), the tail of total reading time (τ), look-backs from later text, and re-reading time; and not reliably positive for typical first-pass reading time (μ) and typical total reading time (μ) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">5</ref>).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that prequestions selectively alter how readers process information relevant to the questions, rather than producing a general increase in processing across the passage.
The distributional analyses provide further insight into the nature of these changes.

Prequestions did not produce a reliable shift in the Gaussian component (μ) of reading times, with Bayes factors favoring the absence of a difference in both first-pass reading and total gaze duration.
Instead, prequestions increased the exponential component (τ), indicating a greater contribution from unusually long reading times.

This pattern suggests that prequestions do not uniformly slow reading of relevant information, but instead alter the distribution in a way consistent with additional processing on some encounters with an answer.
The increased frequency of look-backs and longer rereading times further indicate that readers devoted additional processing to prequestioned information after initially encountering it.
Importantly, these changes were specific to the prequestioned sentences, with no corresponding increase or decrease in processing of non-prequestioned sentences.

This specificity parallels the metaanalytic findings of King-Shepard et al. (2025) and St. Hilaire et al. (2024), who reported a robust specific memory benefit but neither a reliable general benefit nor a general cost.
text.formatted: This specificity parallels the metaanalytic findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">King-Shepard et al. (2025)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">St. Hilaire et al. (2024)</ref>, who reported a robust specific memory benefit but neither a reliable general benefit nor a general cost.

text.text: The absence of changes to non-prequestioned information also provides little support for accounts proposing that prequestions broadly increase attention or monitoring across an entire topic or passage.

One possible explanation for this pattern is that additional processing is triggered when readers recognize that a sentence contains the answer to a prequestion. Lewis and Mensink (2012) proposed a related mechanism in which information that overlaps with a prequestion in wording or meaning "resonates" with the reader's memory of the question, prompting additional inspection.
text.formatted: One possible explanation for this pattern is that additional processing is triggered when readers recognize that a sentence contains the answer to a prequestion. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref> proposed a related mechanism in which information that overlaps with a prequestion in wording or meaning "resonates" with the reader's memory of the question, prompting additional inspection.

text.text: Such recognition may occur only after readers have processed enough of a sentence to identify its relevance.
Moreover, recognition may not occur on every encounter, particularly if readers fail to notice the connection or no longer remember the question.
Consequently, recognition-triggered processing could produce disproportionately long reading times on some occasions rather than a uniform increase in reading duration.
This interpretation is consistent with the increased τ observed in the present study.
Previous distributional research has similarly shown that some experimental manipulations primarily affect the right tail of response-time distributions rather than their location.
For example, modest visual degradation of text has been found to shift μ (White & Staub, 2012), whereas familiarity in scene viewing has been associated with increases in τ (Guy et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For example, modest visual degradation of text has been found to shift μ <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(White & Staub, 2012)</ref>, whereas familiarity in scene viewing has been associated with increases in τ <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Guy et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Although these distributional patterns do not uniquely identify cognitive processes, our findings are consistent with the possibility that recognizing question-relevant information sometimes triggers additional processing.
The timing of the eye-movement effects provides further insight into this possibility.
The increase in τ during first-pass reading suggests that additional processing can occur during the initial encounter with an answer, before readers move on to subsequent text.
At the same time, the greater frequency of look-backs and longer rereading times suggest that readers also return to relevant information after initially encountering it.
These returns may provide opportunities to compare the information with the original prequestion or an earlier guess, resolve uncertainty, or rehearse the answer.
Recognition of the connection between a prequestion and its answer may therefore play an important role in determining when readers allocate additional attention.
Consistent with the importance of remembering prequestions, St. Hilaire and Carpenter (2020) found that prequestions enhanced learning from video lectures only when learners remembered the questions.
text.formatted: Consistent with the importance of remembering prequestions, <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">St. Hilaire and Carpenter (2020)</ref> found that prequestions enhanced learning from video lectures only when learners remembered the questions.

text.text: The present findings are also relevant to the attentional-window account (Sana & Carpenter, 2023), which proposes that attention remains elevated while learners search for an answer and returns to baseline once the answer is found.
text.formatted: The present findings are also relevant to the attentional-window account <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Sana & Carpenter, 2023)</ref>, which proposes that attention remains elevated while learners search for an answer and returns to baseline once the answer is found.

text.text: Although this account can accommodate increased processing while readers search for relevant information, it does not straightforwardly predict the additional look-backs and rereading observed after readers have already encountered the answer.
These findings suggest that the influence of prequestions on visual processing may extend beyond the initial search for relevant information.
More broadly, the results suggest that the benefits of prequestions cannot be explained simply in terms of increased time spent attending to relevant information.
If prequestions produced a uniform slowing of reading, we might expect a broader shift in reading-time distributions.
Instead, the observed effects were concentrated in the right tail and in subsequent returns to the targeted sentences.

This pattern is consistent with the possibility that prequestions influence the processing of relevant information after it has been recognized, rather than merely encouraging readers to allocate more attention to it in advance.

Such an interpretation aligns with the mental model hypothesis proposed by Motz et al. (2026), according to which prequestions activate relevant prior knowledge that facilitates the processing of related information during learning.
text.formatted: Such an interpretation aligns with the mental model hypothesis proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Motz et al. (2026)</ref>, according to which prequestions activate relevant prior knowledge that facilitates the processing of related information during learning.

text.text: On this account, recognizing a connection between incoming information and previously activated knowledge may prompt additional attention or elaboration.
However, the present study cannot determine whether such knowledge activation preceded the observed changes in eye movements.

Furthermore, because the non-prequestioned sentences concerned a different disease, the design cannot establish whether activated knowledge would also facilitate processing of related but non-prequestioned information within the same topic.
The observed pattern is also compatible with metacognitive explanations of the prequestion effect.
By revealing gaps in learners' knowledge, prequestions may encourage monitoring for relevant information during subsequent learning (King-Shepard et al., 2025).
text.formatted: By revealing gaps in learners' knowledge, prequestions may encourage monitoring for relevant information during subsequent learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(King-Shepard et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Recognizing that a sentence provides an answer may prompt learners to evaluate their earlier responses or attend more closely to information they previously could not retrieve.

The longer readings and additional returns observed here are consistent with such monitoring, although eye movements alone cannot distinguish metacognitive evaluation from elaboration, rehearsal, or other forms of additional processing.
Future research combining eye tracking with measures such as judgments of learning or confidence ratings may help differentiate these possibilities (King-Shepard et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Future research combining eye tracking with measures such as judgments of learning or confidence ratings may help differentiate these possibilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(King-Shepard et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the present findings also do not establish that increased processing causes the specific memory benefit.
Because reading behavior was measured rather than experimentally manipulated, the relationship between additional processing and subsequent memory remains correlational.
Prequestions may also strengthen memory through processes that are not directly reflected in eye movements.
Experiments that manipulate opportunities for rereading or returning to previously encountered answers could help determine whether these behaviors contribute causally to the prequestion effect.
The present findings also extend previous eye-tracking research on prequestions.

Because participants in our TB prequestion condition read the same passage used in Experiment 2 of Lewis and Mensink (2012) and received prequestions about the same topic, comparisons between the TB and no-prequestion groups provide a close conceptual replication of that experiment.
text.formatted: Because participants in our TB prequestion condition read the same passage used in Experiment 2 of <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref> and received prequestions about the same topic, comparisons between the TB and no-prequestion groups provide a close conceptual replication of that experiment.

text.text: Consistent with Lewis and Mensink (2012), TB prequestions improved subsequent memory for TB information (11.8 percentage points, 95% CrI [5.3, 17.9]), increased the frequency of look-backs to TB sentences (10.0 percentage points, 95% CrI [3.0, 16.9]), and increased the time spent rereading those sentences (38.6 ms per word, 95% CrI [12.2, 67.1]).
text.formatted: Consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lewis and Mensink (2012)</ref>, TB prequestions improved subsequent memory for TB information (11.8 percentage points, 95% CrI [5.3, 17.9]), increased the frequency of look-backs to TB sentences (10.0 percentage points, 95% CrI [3.0, 16.9]), and increased the time spent rereading those sentences (38.6 ms per word, 95% CrI [12.2, 67.1]).

text.text: However, whereas Lewis and Mensink (2012) found more re-inspection of targeted sentences during first-pass reading, we found no reliable difference in first-pass reading of TB sentences when examining either μ (6.2 ms per word, 95% CrI [-13.9, 26.9]) or τ (7.6 ms per word, 95%

CrI <ref type="bibr">[-19.6, 35.3]</ref>).

text.text: When data were pooled across both prequestion groups, first-pass reading showed an increase in τ without a corresponding shift in μ, although the evidence was weak.
Several methodological differences may contribute to the discrepancies between studies.
The present study included a larger sample and counterbalanced the targeted content, allowing us to compare reading of the same sentences with and without prequestions.

We also measured rereading as time spent on a sentence after the reader had progressed beyond it, and operationalized first-pass processing using selective regression-path duration (Schotter & Dillon, 2025).
text.formatted: We also measured rereading as time spent on a sentence after the reader had progressed beyond it, and operationalized first-pass processing using selective regression-path duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Schotter & Dillon, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This measure was particularly useful because approximately half of first passes were interrupted by brief returns to the preceding line.
In addition, the distributional analyses allowed us to distinguish changes in the Gaussian and exponential components of reading times, which cannot be separated through analyses of means alone.

This distinction is important because a difference in average reading time can arise from different changes in the underlying distribution, with potentially different implications for how prequestions influence reading.
Our findings also resemble those of Bostan and Ozcelik (2026), who observed more fixations on prequestioned sentences and more transitions between them.
text.formatted: Our findings also resemble those of <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bostan and Ozcelik (2026)</ref>, who observed more fixations on prequestioned sentences and more transitions between them.

text.text: These patterns are broadly consistent with the increased look-backs and rereading observed here.
However, unlike the present study and much of the prequestion literature, Bostan and Ozcelik (2026) also reported a general memory benefit.
text.formatted: However, unlike the present study and much of the prequestion literature, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bostan and Ozcelik (2026)</ref> also reported a general memory benefit.

text.text: One possible explanation concerns the types of prequestions used.

Their integrative questions required readers to combine information distributed across different parts of the passage, potentially encouraging processing of information beyond the sentences directly targeted by the questions (Pan & Carpenter, 2023).
text.formatted: Their integrative questions required readers to combine information distributed across different parts of the passage, potentially encouraging processing of information beyond the sentences directly targeted by the questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Pan & Carpenter, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the prequestions used in the present study targeted individual facts contained within single sentences, and neither memory nor eye movements showed reliable general benefits.
This difference is consistent with the possibility that the scope of attentional processing depends on the information required to answer the prequestions.
However, given the relatively small sample in Bostan and Ozcelik (2026) (12 participants per group), this explanation remains tentative.
More broadly, these findings highlight the importance of selecting appropriate statistical analyses when examining eye-tracking data.
Reading-time distributions are typically rightskewed, and experimental manipulations may affect different parts of these distributions in different ways.

Conventional analyses of mean reading times can identify overall differences between conditions but cannot distinguish a general shift in reading times from a change in the right tail of the distribution.
In the present study, the ex-Gaussian analyses revealed that prequestions increased the exponential component (τ) of reading times without a corresponding shift in the Gaussian component (μ).
This distinction would not have been apparent from analyses of means alone.

Thus, distributional analyses can provide a more detailed characterization of how experimental manipulations influence reading behavior, revealing patterns that may otherwise be overlooked or obscured by conventional approaches.
One limitation of the present study concerns the characteristics of the reading materials.
Each topic was represented by only five target sentences and five final-test questions.

Moreover, the Polio and TB sentences differed in length, reading difficulty, content, and position within the passage.irst, each topic was represented by only five target sentences and five final-test questions.
Moreover, the Polio and TB sentences differed in length, reading difficulty, content, and position within the passage.

These differences are particularly important in eye-tracking research, where linguistic and visual characteristics of the text can influence fixation durations, regressions, and rereading independently of the experimental manipulation.
Consequently, differences in eye movements between topics cannot necessarily be attributed to prequestions alone.
To address this concern, our primary analyses compared the same sentences across conditions, allowing us to account for fixed characteristics of the sentences themselves.
Nevertheless, the effects were not identical across topics.
In particular, increases in look-backs and rereading were driven primarily by the TB prequestion group, whose target sentences also attracted more look-backs in the noprequestion condition.
These findings underscore the importance of carefully controlling text stimuli in eye-tracking research.

Future studies should more closely match target sentences on relevant linguistic and visual characteristics, including sentence length, syntactic complexity, reading difficulty, and position within the passage, or systematically counterbalance which sentences are targeted by prequestions across versions of the same text.
In summary, prequestions selectively changed how readers processed information that answered the questions.

Rather than producing a uniform slowing of reading, prequestions increased the contribution of unusually long reading times and prompted readers to return to relevant information more frequently and for longer periods.
These effects were restricted to prequestioned sentences and accompanied a specific memory benefit, with no reliable general benefit.
The pattern is consistent with the possibility that recognizing information as relevant to a prequestion triggers additional processing during initial reading and subsequent rereading.
However, whether such processing contributes causally to improved memory, or instead accompanies other learning mechanisms initiated by prequestions, remains an open question.

text.text: Each fixation was assigned to a text line after correcting for vertical drift, separately for each reader and page.

The correction combines two approaches used in automated driftcorrection algorithms (Carr et al., 2022): assigning sequences of fixations to a line together, and modelling drift as a function of position on the page.
text.formatted: The correction combines two approaches used in automated driftcorrection algorithms <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Carr et al., 2022)</ref>: assigning sequences of fixations to a line together, and modelling drift as a function of position on the page.

text.text: First, a single vertical offset was estimated: candidate shifts of the recorded positions were tried in steps of 0.05 line spacings, and the shift that minimized the summed squared distance between each fixation and its nearest text line was kept (distances were capped at one line spacing, so that stray fixations in the margins had little influence).

Second, consecutive fixations moving along a line were grouped into chains; a chain ended at a horizontal jump larger than 10% of the screen width (e.g., a return sweep to the next line) or a vertical jump larger than 0.6 line spacings.
Each chain was assigned as a whole to the text line nearest its median position, so that a single fixation drifting toward a neighbouring line stayed on the line being read.

Third, because drift often grew down the page or across it, a linear model of the recorded vertical position as a function of the assigned line's position and the fixation's horizontal position (recorded y = a + b × line y + c × x) was fitted to fixations whose chain lay within half a line spacing of its line; gaze positions were corrected by inverting this model and the chains were reassigned, and this was repeated five times.
The linear model was used only if it was plausible (a vertical stretch within 20% and a tilt of less than one line across the screen); otherwise the single offset was kept.

Throughout, the correction was limited everywhere on the page to the calibration accuracy criterion of 0.5° (0.57 cm, about 0.45 of a line spacing), so it could not move a reader's gaze by a whole line.
Chains more than half a line spacing from every text line were treated as off the text.
